readings.title: A square with room to sit
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town proposed new seats in its central square. The first drawing arranged benches neatly around a fountain, but residents described different habits. The central difficulty was seats placed away from ordinary routes. Older visitors wanted somewhere to rest between shops, while parents watched children from a shaded edge of the square. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried temporary seats at several positions. Planners moved lightweight chairs during a trial and observed where people stopped without blocking a busy walkway. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed shade and walking distance shaped use. Chairs close to the fountain looked attractive in drawings but remained empty during hot afternoons. In response, the group adopted benches near shade and clear paths. The council selected locations that offered rest while leaving enough space for pedestrians and wheelchair users. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: public space should follow everyday movement. A pleasant square is shaped not just by symmetry but by the routes and needs of the people who spend time there. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a square with room to sit, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Library hours for changing work patterns
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A district library considered staying open later on weekdays. Staff had limited hours, so a longer day would require closing at another time. The central difficulty was uncertain demand for evening visits. Some learners wanted quiet study after work, while parents valued an earlier weekend period with children. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a short trial of two schedules. The library tested a later weekday opening and an additional Saturday hour, recording visits and asking what people used the time for. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed Saturday family visits exceeded expectations. Evening study mattered to a smaller group, but children’s activities filled the new weekend hour consistently. In response, the group adopted a mixed schedule reviewed each season. Managers kept one later weekday and the extra Saturday period, then promised to reconsider both after seasonal demand changed. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: opening hours should reflect varied users. The library could not extend every day, but it could use evidence to balance the needs of learners and families. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in library hours for changing work patterns, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: A bus shelter designed for waiting
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A village planned a new shelter beside its busiest bus stop. A standard design protected against rain but faced away from approaching buses. The central difficulty was a shelter with a poor view of the road. Passengers worried they would have to step into the rain to see a bus coming around the bend. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a temporary frame at the stop. The council marked the proposed shelter size and asked passengers to stand in it during different weather and traffic conditions. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed visibility mattered alongside weather protection. People wanted cover, yet they also needed to notice a bus early enough to signal the driver safely. In response, the group adopted a revised opening and seating position. Designers turned the front slightly and placed a seat where waiting passengers could watch the road without blocking the entrance. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: small design details affect public confidence. A shelter succeeds when people can wait comfortably and understand what is happening around them. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in a bus shelter designed for waiting, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Young residents shape a town meeting
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town council wanted more young adults at planning meetings. It invited them through the usual weekday notice but received few replies. The central difficulty was meeting times clashing with work and study. Some residents had evening classes or shifts, and the invitation used formal language without explaining what decisions were open. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried short conversations at varied locations. Council workers visited a training centre and a sports club, asking which issues mattered and how people preferred to respond. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed clear choices encouraged more useful comments. Participants were more willing to discuss specific proposals than to attend a broad meeting with an unclear purpose. In response, the group adopted a focused session and written response option. The council published two concrete questions, held a weekend discussion and accepted comments from those who could not attend. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: participation improves when its purpose is visible. Inviting people requires more than announcing a date; they need to know how their experience can influence a decision. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in young residents shape a town meeting, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A public square may look balanced in a drawing while offering little comfort to the people who use it. One town planned benches around a fountain. Residents pointed out that older visitors needed places to rest between shops and that parents wanted shade while watching children. Planners placed temporary chairs in different parts of the square and observed where people sat. The chairs nearest the fountain were often empty during hot afternoons. The final plan put benches near shade without blocking walking routes. The trial showed that the best place for a seat depends on daily movement and weather, not only on the appearance of a plan.
translation.explanation: 注意while对照关系与not only的表达。
translation.referenceAnswer: 公共广场在图纸上可能看起来很均衡，却无法让使用它的人感到舒适。一个城镇计划在喷泉周围放置长椅。居民指出，年长的访客需要在商店之间休息，家长则希望在阴凉处照看孩子。规划人员在广场不同位置放置临时椅子，观察人们坐在哪里。炎热的下午，最靠近喷泉的椅子常常空着。最终方案把长椅放在阴凉处，同时不挡住步行路线。试行表明，座椅的最佳位置取决于日常行走与天气，而不只是设计图的外观。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a town council proposing where to place seats in a public square. Describe a temporary trial, whose needs should be considered, and how the council should choose final locations.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖临时试摆、多群体需求和最终选址依据。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Council Members,
New seats would make the square more welcoming, but I hope their positions will be chosen through a short trial. The council could place movable chairs near the shops, the fountain and the shaded side for two weeks. Staff should observe where people choose to rest at different times, especially during hot afternoons. They should also check that the chairs do not block wheelchair users or busy walking routes.
Please invite comments from older visitors, parents with children and people who cross the square on their way to work. Their reasons for choosing a place may be more useful than a simple count of occupied seats. The final plan should provide shade and convenient rests while keeping a clear route through the square. A public explanation would show how the trial influenced the decision.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
